content: 1. The second edition of the mutation catalog introduced new symbols to denote mutations that were newly identified (NEW), downgraded (DOWN), upgraded (UP), or changed in their association with resistance (SWITCH). Mutations that remained unchanged between the two editions were also noted. 2. A new method for annotating insertions and deletions (indels) was adopted in the second edition, making direct comparisons with the first edition impossible for these variants. 3. For rifampicin (RIF) and rifapentine (RPT), the mutations rpoB Val170Phe and Ile491Phe remained the only markers of resistance outside the rifampin resistance-determining region (RRDR), which spans rpoB codons 426–452. 4. The WHO-endorsed GenoScreen Deeplex® Myc-TB assay, based on Illumina sequencing, does not detect minority variants below 10% frequency at nucleotide 1346 of rpoB due to the noisy nature of this position. External quality assessments have questioned the validity of T-to-A changes at rpoB Leu449Gln, suggesting potential issues with library preparation, sequencing, or contamination. 5. Any rpoB changes at codon 449 identified by Illumina sequencing, particularly if unfixed, should be carefully analyzed to avoid overcalling RIF resistance. Codon 449 falls within the RRDR and is subject to additional grading rules. 6. The WHO has previously endorsed the use of RIF as a surrogate for RPT, meaning that the classifications for RIF resistance also apply to RPT. 7. The second edition excluded in-frame mutations from the additional grading rule for katG mutations, as these are less likely to abolish katG function. All katG mutations were assumed to confer high-level isoniazid (INH) resistance, while inhA mutations were considered to confer low-level resistance unless combined with other mutations. 8. Rare katG mutations that do not meet standard resistance classification criteria were explored using relaxed criteria, similar to those applied to pncA mutations. These analyses suggest that only a small proportion of sensitivity issues in the dataset were due to katG resistance mutations. 9. For ethambutol (EMB), 13 non-synonymous mutations in embB and one intergenic mutation upstream of embA met the criteria for Group 1 mutations. No Group 2 mutations were identified. Reduced specificity for embB mutations may be due to minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) close to the critical concentration (CC), leading to poor agreement with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (pDST). 10. Two resistance markers from the first edition (embA -12C>T and embB Leu74Arg) were downgraded to Group 3 in the second edition, suggesting a minimal role of heteroresistance. 11. For pyrazinamide (PZA), only pncA mutations were classified as resistance markers. In-frame pncA mutations, such as Gly113_Leu116delinsVal, were excluded from the loss-of-function (LoF) grading rule in the second edition, confirming that in-frame indels are less likely to be markers of resistance. 12. Most Mycobacterium bovis isolates are intrinsically resistant to PZA due to the Group 1 pncA His57Asp mutation. Similarly, Mycobacterium canettii, which is rarely found outside the Horn of Africa, is intrinsically PZA-resistant. The genetic basis for this phenotype in M. canettii remains unclear, as most isolates lack plausible pncA resistance mutations. 13. Identification of M. canettii should ideally rely on multiple phylogenetically informative mutations in genes not under selection. However, the choice of markers depends on the genomic regions interrogated by the assay. 14. The synonymous mutation 138A>G at codon 46 of pncA, proposed as a marker for M. canettii in the literature, was also observed in some lineage 4 Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) isolates. As a result, it was not endorsed as a marker for inferring intrinsic resistance.
